input: This summary reviews the delivery performance of a contract packaging firm that operates 3 plants and generates revenue of $60 million per year. The analysis draws on the firm's order records for 12 months, encompassing no fewer than 15733 orders, and the picture that emerges is a concerning one. Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery stood at 86%, which falls noticeably short of the target of 95% that the firm has set itself. At the same time, the order backlog has grown to 3.2 weeks, compared with 2.1 weeks a year ago, and the cost of overtime reached $1.7 million last year, an increase of 22% on the year before. A closer examination of the data reveals that the problem is far from evenly spread: Plant 2 accounts for 58% of all late orders, which strongly suggests that the difficulties are concentrated in one location rather than systemic. Against this background, a scheduling system covering all plants has been quoted at $351k, while Plant 2 alone would cost $157k. An internal estimate — not a vendor figure, and therefore to be treated with some caution — suggests that overtime at Plant 2 could be reduced by 15–20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration is accordingly to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported, with the operations director owning the scheduling programme.
target: Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported; the operations director owns the scheduling programme. The firm is a contract packaging business, and delivery reliability is the term on which its contracts are renewed. The evidence base is order records for 12 months, covering 15733 orders across the firm's 3 plants, which take $60 million of revenue per year. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 86%, against a target of 95%. The two-quarter figure is the current run rate, measured against the same target the contracts carry. The order backlog stands at 3.2 weeks, against 2.1 weeks a year ago, and overtime cost was $1.7 million last year, up 22% on the year before. Overtime is the mechanism by which the plants currently protect delivery dates, and its cost is the price of the present shortfall. Late orders concentrate at Plant 2, which accounts for 58% of them. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $351k; Plant 2 alone is $157k, so the staged installation commits the smaller sum against the plant that carries most of the lateness. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15–20% in the first year. The staged route also bounds the commitment: if the results fall short of the estimate, the remaining plants have not yet been committed.
